power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

The population in many countries, particularly in Western societies, is ageing.
With decreasing fertility, fewer young workers are starting to take part in the labour market.
Current cohorts of middle-aged and older workers are expected to and likely to be working longer than previous birth cohorts were (Hess et al., 2021).

text.text: Furthermore, due to shortages of qualified applicants, employer are increasingly interested to keep their older, experienced workers in the company, and effects of typical HR practices on employee behaviour and well-being seem to change with age (Kooij et al., 2013).

text.text: All these developments make it even more important to understand what contributes to work satisfaction of aging workers (Hertel & Zacher, 2018).

text.text: Studies commonly found that older workers are more satisfied with their work than younger workers (Ng & Feldman, 2010).

text.text: However, most of these studies were of cross-sectional nature and in convenience samples and the results may thus be overly optimistic.
It is therefore important to investigate typical age-related trajectories of job satisfaction over time, before testing what characterizes more or less optimal developments (Zacher, 2015).

text.text: Consequently, the first aim in the present study is to examine how work satisfaction changed over nine years in a population-based sample of German workers aged 40-59 at baseline.
Second, we considered the role of the tendency to engage in flexible goal adjustment (Brandtstädter & Renner, 1990; Tolentino et al., 2013).

text.text: We tested for its association with level and change in work satisfaction because of its role for informing ways to keep older workers motivated and satisfied in an ageing workforce.
With the increased aging of the workforce, it becomes more important than ever to study the aging worker's experiences at the work place.
In the previous decade, research on "successful aging at work" has grown immensely.

The most influential conceptualizations have been developed by Kooij (2015) and Zacher (2015). Kooij (2015) argued that successful aging at work means the maintenance of health, work motivation, and work ability over the work life span.

text.text: Workers need to proactively adapt to their environment to ensure personenvironment fit to achieve these outcomes, for example via job crafting or coping behaviors.
In contrast, Zacher (2015) defined successful aging as experiencing above-average trajectories of important outcomes such as work satisfaction or performance.

text.text: Research based on Kooij's (2015) model has mainly focused on the adaptive actions of workers to ensure personenvironment fit, whereas research based on Zacher's (2015) model has mainly focused on predictors of above-average trajectories of work-related outcomes (Zacher et al., 2018).

text.text: In the present study, we will contribute to both models: Based on Zacher's (2015) approach, we were interested in the typical age-related trajectory of work satisfaction, and what predicts deviations from the typical trajectory.
However, in line with Kooij's (2015) approach, we consider a potential way to achieve person-environment fit -flexible goal adjustment (Brandtstädter & Renner, 1990).

text.text: Age-related changes, for example with regard to cognitive performance (Fisher et al., 2019) or emotion regulation (Scheibe et al., 2016) present particular challenges and opportunities for reaching satisfaction with the job.

text.text: Nevertheless, a meta-analysis, including both cross-sectional and (to a smaller degree) longitudinal studies, showed that like other work attitudes, job satisfaction shows a positive association with age (Ng & Feldman, 2010).

text.text: The authors explain these findings with age-related changes in priorities, in line with socioemotional selectivity theory (Carstensen et al., 2003): With increasing age, people perceive their time as more limited, which leads to motivational changes.

text.text: Older adults should therefore prefer immediate gratification from intrinsic parts of the job (e.g., social interactions, or pleasurable work tasks) over long-term benefits such as promotion or knowledge acquisition (Kooij et al., 2011).

text.text: This would secure them maintained work satisfaction at work.

Furthermore, older adults are more focused on experiencing positive emotions and avoiding negative ones than younger adults, and also seem to be better at emotion regulation (Scheibe et al., 2016), which should all help them to stay or become satisfied.

text.text: Likewise, and of particular importance for our study, authors have assumed that with older age, workers are more likely to engage in secondary control strategies (Kooij et al., 2011), which is a term from the motivational life span theory (Heckhausen et al., 2010).

text.text: The theory implies that people strive to bring their situation in line with their goals and interests (primary control).

In the face of increasing constraints, older workers should be more likely than younger workers to engage in strategies such as "managing the attractiveness of chosen goals, providing rationale for disengaging from nonchosen courses of actions, or bolstering perceptions of competence" (Rudolph, 2016, p. 142), which also in turns increases the chance to perceive primary control.

text.text: Finally, over the work life span, workers are likely to search for more satisfying jobs and to leave those jobs that are not fulfilling their needs.
All of these factors should contribute to increases in job satisfaction over the work life span.
However, it has been noted that most studies in the field are cross-sectional (Ng & Feldman, 2010).

text.text: Furthermore, studies have often included a very large age-span, so it is unclear which phases of the work life span are associated with particular changes.
In the current study, we study change in job satisfaction over nine years among workers who were aged 40-59 at baseline.
These individuals were in midlife ("roughly 40-59", Lachman, 2015, p. 327) at baseline.
Although the stereotypical "midlife crisis" seems to be not very common (Lachman, 2015), midlife is an important period in life with particular challenges and opportunities (Infurna et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Although the stereotypical "midlife crisis" seems to be not very common <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Lachman, 2015)</ref>, midlife is an important period in life with particular challenges and opportunities <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Infurna et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Individuals in midlife need to balance multiple roles, for example because of apart from managing their own career, workers are often needed to mentor younger co-workers, take care of children, grandchildren or ill family members (Infurna et al., 2020).

text.text: Furthermore, midlife has been conceptualized as a pivotal period, as development in midlife is shaped by earlier developments but also sets the stage for late life developments in terms of health and wellbeing (Infurna et al., 2020; Lachman et al., 2014).

text.text: It is therefore important to understand how individual job satisfaction develops in this period, and what contributes to interindividual differences in this development.
In line with previous research, we assume H1.
There is a positive association of age and higher job satisfaction at baseline.

text.text: As noted above, Kooij (2015) emphasizes that workers need to engage in behaviours improving individual person-environment fit at work.

text.text: Ageing workers are likely to experience that some of their goals (e.g., promotion) are not attainable, or become less attainable over time, which may decrease this fit and endanger successful aging at work and work satisfaction.
Therefore, workers are required to engage in proactive or adaptive goal (dis-)engagement strategies (Kooij et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Therefore, workers are required to engage in proactive or adaptive goal (dis-)engagement strategies <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Kooij et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Such strategies can be found in the dual-process model of assimilative and accommodative coping (Brandtstädter & Rothermund, 2002), which is a lifespan theory, describing self-regulation over the lifespan and which bears some similarities with the motivational lifespan theory (Heckhausen et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Such strategies can be found in the dual-process model of assimilative and accommodative coping <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Brandtstädter & Rothermund, 2002)</ref>, which is a lifespan theory, describing self-regulation over the lifespan and which bears some similarities with the motivational lifespan theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Heckhausen et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Assimilative coping means to bring the environment in line with one's goals (also called tenacious goal pursuit).
Accommodative coping, on the other hand, means to flexibly adjust ones goals and preferences in line with situational opportunities (Brandtstädter & Renner, 1990).
text.formatted: Accommodative coping, on the other hand, means to flexibly adjust ones goals and preferences in line with situational opportunities <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Brandtstädter & Renner, 1990)</ref>.

text.text: Successful coping over the lifespan is reached in the situation-specific interplay of both strategies.
In the current study, we focus on accommodative coping, which may be particularly important in the context of balancing family and work roles in midlife.
Adjusting one's career goals and following those goals that are attainable while maintaining a satisfying family life may be necessary to remain satisfied with work over time.
The use of accommodative coping seems to become more frequent with age (Brandtstädter & Renner, 1990).

text.text: We assume that flexible goal adjustment is important to remain satisfied with one's work place in midlife, when many workers try to balance family life, care work and occupation, and for some, first physical health problems set in.
Given previous results, we expect H3: Flexible goal adjustment is associated with higher job satisfaction at baseline.

In the present study, we included the waves in 2008, 2011 and 2014 and 2017, because flexible goal adjustment was not assessed before 2008 and later waves were conducted during the Covid-19 pandemic, which may have affected work satisfaction in various ways that would be beyond the scope of the present paper.
Individuals aged 40-59 at baseline were included to capture developments in midlife.

We further only included the baseline sample in 2008 to increase the representativeness of the study sample, as the inclusion of those participating already in 1996 or 2002 would have made the older part of the sample more selective than the younger (as the survey only starts at age 40).
We only included individuals who were working at baseline in 2008 (N = 2,106).
One individual never reported work satisfaction and was thus excluded from the study samples.
We included data from all remaining n = 2,105 in our analyses to achieve as unbiased estimates as possible, at least for information on the level of job satisfaction.
Of those, n = 1,034 took part in the survey in 2011, n = 1,016 in 2014 and n = 893 in 2017.

text.text: Work satisfaction, our dependent variable, was assessed by one item from a list of attitudes toward work: "How satisfied are you with your work as a whole".
Response alternatives were very satisfied (1), satisfied (2), yes and no (3), dissatisfied (4), very dissatisfied (5).
We recoded the item so higher scores meant higher satisfaction.

No validated work satisfaction scale is included in the DEAS, but single-item measures of work satisfaction and other work-related constructs usually show very good reliability and validity (Matthews et al., 2022; Nagy, 2002).

Age was included as a linear variable, and was centered around age 40.

Flexible goal adjustment was assessed with a 10-item short form of the flexible goal adjustment scale (Brandtstädter & Renner, 1990), which has been used in previous studies with the DEAS (Wettstein et al., 2020).

text.text: Ten items (e.g., "Faced with a disappointment, I remind myself that other things in life are just as important") were rated from strongly agree (1) to strongly disagree (5).
We recoded the items, so higher scores meant higher agreement, and we used mean scores.
Cronbach's alpha reliability was α = .81.
Covariates.
We controlled for gender, education, as well as physical and mental health.
Gender was used as a dichotomous variable (0 = man,1 = woman).
Education was assessed based on ISCED categories, but we dichotomized the item with 1 corresponding to high (tertiary) education.

text.text: Interestingly, change in work satisfaction was not to related to health, depressive symptoms, education or gender.
In the present study, we studied predictors of level and nine-year changes in work satisfaction in a sample of German workers who were in midlife at baseline.

Midlife is an understudied period in life, although it is an important time when individuals need to balance their work life and private life while being engaged in different roles (Infurna et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Midlife is an understudied period in life, although it is an important time when individuals need to balance their work life and private life while being engaged in different roles <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Infurna et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Building on research on successful aging at work (Kooij et al., 2020), our focus was on the role of age and flexible goal adjustment.
text.formatted: Building on research on successful aging at work <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Kooij et al., 2020)</ref>, our focus was on the role of age and flexible goal adjustment.

text.text: Our results show that work satisfaction, on average, is stable across midlife and that flexible goal adjustment is associated with levels, but not changes over time.
Previous studies have repeatedly shown positive effects of age on work satisfaction (Ng & Feldman, 2010).
text.formatted: Previous studies have repeatedly shown positive effects of age on work satisfaction <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Ng & Feldman, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: In our analyses, however, older age was not related to levels or changes in work satisfaction across midlife.

This is in line with a recent study with a different German dataset than the one we used in the present study, which showed that there may be distinct declines at the end of one's working life, after an initial period of stability in Germany (Henning et al., 2024).
text.formatted: This is in line with a recent study with a different German dataset than the one we used in the present study, which showed that there may be distinct declines at the end of one's working life, after an initial period of stability in Germany <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Henning et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: It is unclear how generalizable the age differences are to other countries: Previous studies showed that job satisfaction levels differ between countries (Drabe et al., 2015).
text.formatted: It is unclear how generalizable the age differences are to other countries: Previous studies showed that job satisfaction levels differ between countries <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Drabe et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Different levels of job satisfaction can be partly explained by socioeconomic and differences, but also by varying cultural values and standards for what constitutes particular levels of job satisfaction (Drabe et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Different levels of job satisfaction can be partly explained by socioeconomic and differences, but also by varying cultural values and standards for what constitutes particular levels of job satisfaction <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Drabe et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, while a positive relationship between age and job satisfaction has been established in the literature, it was shown to be moderated by national context (Tay et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Furthermore, while a positive relationship between age and job satisfaction has been established in the literature, it was shown to be moderated by national context <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Tay et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Germany is individualistic and has a pronounced social security system, which may explain that such factors as job security are less important for job satisfaction than in other countries, while having an interesting job or good relationship with colleagues are quite important for job satisfaction (Drabe et al., 2015; Olsen et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Germany is individualistic and has a pronounced social security system, which may explain that such factors as job security are less important for job satisfaction than in other countries, while having an interesting job or good relationship with colleagues are quite important for job satisfaction <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Drabe et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Olsen et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Of further relevance for older workers may be its retirement policies, with a statutory retirement age, as well as the socalled "early exit" culture with workers often trying to retire as early as their financial situation allows it (Ebener et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Of further relevance for older workers may be its retirement policies, with a statutory retirement age, as well as the socalled "early exit" culture with workers often trying to retire as early as their financial situation allows it <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Ebener et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Cross-cultural research is needed to understand the universality of within-person change or stability in job satisfaction in midlife.

Accommodation, or more specifically, flexible goal adjustment, which is the ability to easily adjust or drop one's goals if they are not reachable anymore, or if continuing to follow them would be maladaptive for the individual, is commonly associated with better well-being outcomes (Bailly et al., 2012) and also likely to be helpful for the work experience (Tolentino et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Accommodation, or more specifically, flexible goal adjustment, which is the ability to easily adjust or drop one's goals if they are not reachable anymore, or if continuing to follow them would be maladaptive for the individual, is commonly associated with better well-being outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Bailly et al., 2012)</ref> and also likely to be helpful for the work experience <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Tolentino et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: However, we found only a significant cross-sectional association, but flexible goal adjustment did not predict changes in work satisfaction.
One reason may be that the variance in change was rather small and none of our predictors, apart from age, did significantly predict change in work satisfaction.
Flexible goal adjustment may also predict changes over shorter time spans, which could be assessed in daily diary studies (Scheibe et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Flexible goal adjustment may also predict changes over shorter time spans, which could be assessed in daily diary studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Scheibe et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Comparable studies have been conducted with related concepts (i.e., selection, optimization and compensation, (Knecht & Freund, 2017)) among older adults before, but not in the work context.
text.formatted: Comparable studies have been conducted with related concepts (i.e., selection, optimization and compensation, <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Knecht & Freund, 2017)</ref>) among older adults before, but not in the work context.

text.text: Furthermore, it may be stable or even improved goal adjustment, not baseline level, which matters for work satisfaction.
Unfortunately, goal adjustment was not available at all waves, so we could not compute a parallel growth curve model to study slopeslope associations.
Future studies with longitudinal assessments of both work satisfaction and flexible goal adjustment may test at a possible bidirectional, longitudinal relationship.
Fostering job satisfaction over the working life span is an important goal for researchers in the field of aging and work.

As a consequence of the demographic developments, the work force is ageing, which makes it even more important to understand how job satisfaction typically develops, and what contributes to a fulfilling working life for middle-aged and older workers.
Our results show that in a representative sample of middleaged German workers, work satisfaction was rather high and remained so over the course of the study.
Nevertheless, more research is needed to understand when and for whom work satisfaction changes in midlife, and how life events and non-work roles contribute to work satisfaction.
For example, there is only very scarce research of family care for job satisfaction (Stewart, 2013).
text.formatted: For example, there is only very scarce research of family care for job satisfaction <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Stewart, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Although we did not find that flexible goal adjustment was associated with increases in satisfaction over time, we still believe that the distinction of assimilative and accommodative coping can be helpful for future research.
Assimilation (i.e., tenacious goal pursuit) was not measured in our study, but future studies could test how both strategies contribute to long-term change in job satisfaction.

Furthermore, diary or measurement burst studies may help to understand the interplay of accommodation and assimilation in everyday work life, and its short-and long-term consequences for performance and job satisfaction.
The present study is one of very few studies on longitudinal change in work satisfaction across several years in midlife, using a large sample from representative survey data.
Furthermore, to our knowledge, this is the first attempt to study the association of flexible goal adjustment and work satisfaction with longitudinal data (Rudolph, 2016).
text.formatted: Furthermore, to our knowledge, this is the first attempt to study the association of flexible goal adjustment and work satisfaction with longitudinal data <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Rudolph, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Limitations of our study include the large attrition rate over time, as well as the small number of measurements.
Furthermore, our data did not allow us to run a parallel growth curve model, as flexible goal adjustment was not available at all waves.
We also have a large agespan in the sample, which may obscure particular changes in specific phases, for example close to retirement (Henning et al., 2024).
text.formatted: We also have a large agespan in the sample, which may obscure particular changes in specific phases, for example close to retirement <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Henning et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, only flexible goal adjustment, not tenacious goal pursuit, the other adjustment mode in the dual-process model, was included in our data set.
In general, the psychometric qualities of the original scales have been questioned (Henselmans et al., 2011), which is why we use a modified scale in the present study (Wettstein et al., 2020).
text.formatted: In general, the psychometric qualities of the original scales have been questioned <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Henselmans et al., 2011)</ref>, which is why we use a modified scale in the present study <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Wettstein et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Taken together, our results show that the longitudinal relation of age and work satisfaction is complicated and likely non-linear (Hochwarter et al., 2001).
text.formatted: Taken together, our results show that the longitudinal relation of age and work satisfaction is complicated and likely non-linear <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Hochwarter et al., 2001)</ref>.

text.text: Future studies may benefit from taken a more detailed look at different phases such as the time directly after job entry or close to retirement, (Henning et al., 2023; 2024), as well as the effects of engagement in non-work roles (Stewart, 2013).
text.formatted: Future studies may benefit from taken a more detailed look at different phases such as the time directly after job entry or close to retirement, <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Henning et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">2024)</ref>, as well as the effects of engagement in non-work roles <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Stewart, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: To cast more light on the role of flexible goal adjustment for a satisfying work experience, studies with work-specific scales and longitudinal measures of adjustment are needed.
